keywords: measures of kurtosis and tail weight

paper.summary: Moment measures of skewness and kurtosis are driven by the tails: one extreme value can dominate them. We propose shape coefficients built on the half central moment, the expected square root of the deviation from the mean. Negative deviations have imaginary roots, so its real part collects the deviations above the mean and its imaginary part those below. The Asymmetry coefficient, from the angle of this moment, lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$; it is determined by the probability on each side of the mean and by how evenly the deviations spread on each side, and it places the mean as an $L_{1.5}$-quantile. Hypotailedness, the absolute half moment scaled by the square root of the standard deviation, and the Extremity coefficient derived from it measure, as kurtosis does, how far the squared standardised deviations spread from one, but give values near the mean more weight and values in the tails less. We derive the influence functions, showing that they grow linearly for Asymmetry and quadratically for Hypotailedness. We also derive the sharp lower bound of the sample Hypotailedness, the asymptotic normality of the sample coefficients, and closed forms for seven standard distributions. In simulations we show that the sample Asymmetry is nearly unbiased, while Hypotailedness is biased upwards in small samples. Finally, we demonstrate the measures on petroleum rock samples and on daily returns of four European stock indices.

definitions.definition: The half central moment (HCM) of a variable $y$ with finite mean $\mu_1$: $$\mu_{0.5} = \mathrm{E}\left[(y - \mu_1)^{0.5}\right]$$, the square root taken as the principal root, so that $$\mu_{0.5} = \mathrm{E}\left[(y-\mu_1)_+^{0.5}\right] + i\,\mathrm{E}\left[(\mu_1-y)_+^{0.5}\right]$$: the real part $\mathcal{R}$ comes from the values above the mean and the imaginary part $\mathcal{I}$ from those below it. Sample estimate: $$m_{0.5} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} (y_j - m_1)^{0.5}$$, with $m_1$ the sample mean.

The half absolute moment (HAM): $$\nu_{0.5} = \mathcal{R}(\mu_{0.5}) + \mathcal{I}(\mu_{0.5}) = \mathrm{E}|y - \mu_1|^{0.5}$$; sample estimate $$v_{0.5} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} |y_j - m_1|^{0.5}$$.

$$\mathrm{Asymmetry} = 1 - \frac{4\phi}{\pi} = \frac{4}{\pi}\arctan\left(\frac{\mathcal{R}(\mu_{0.5}) - \mathcal{I}(\mu_{0.5})}{\nu_{0.5}}\right),$$ where $\phi = \mathrm{Arg}(\mu_{0.5}) \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; positive when the part above the mean is the larger. The sample coefficient uses $m_{0.5}$ and $v_{0.5}$.

$\mathrm{Hypotailedness} = \frac{\nu_{0.5}}{\sigma^{0.5}}$ for a variable with finite positive variance $\sigma^2$; the sample coefficient divides $v_{0.5}$ by $\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}(y_j - m_1)^2\right)^{0.25}$.
$\mathrm{Extremity} = 2\,\mathrm{Hypotailedness}^{p} - 1$ with $p = \frac{\log 0.5}{\log(2 \times 3^{-0.75})} \approx 5.30$, so that the uniform distribution has Extremity 0.
$\mathrm{CH} = \frac{\mu_{0.5}}{\sigma^{0.5}}$, the half central moment divided by the square root of the standard deviation (the manuscript of 19 November 2026).

For a variable with finite variance and deviation $D = y - \mu_1$: $$H_+ = \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[D^{0.5} \mid D > 0\right]}{\left(\mathrm{E}\left[D^2 \mid D > 0\right]\right)^{0.25}}$$ above the mean and $$H_- = \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[|D|^{0.5} \mid D < 0\right]}{\left(\mathrm{E}\left[D^2 \mid D < 0\right]\right)^{0.25}}$$ below it; in a sample, the same ratios over the values above and below the sample mean.

The bounded Complex Extremity proposed in this study: $\mathrm{CE} = \left(2H_+^{p} - 1\right) + i\left(2H_-^{p} - 1\right)$, with $H_\pm$ the one-sided Hypotailedness and $p = \frac{\log 0.5}{\log(2 \times 3^{-0.75})}$; the real part describes the values above the mean.
The standardised third central moment $\frac{\mathrm{E}[(y-\mu_1)^3]}{\sigma^3}$; sample version with $\frac{1}{n}$ moments.
The standardised fourth central moment minus 3, $\frac{\mathrm{E}[(y-\mu_1)^4]}{\sigma^4} - 3$; sample version with $\frac{1}{n}$ moments.
The L-moment ratio $\tau_3 = \frac{\lambda_3}{\lambda_2}$; sample version from unbiased probability-weighted moments.
The L-moment ratio $\tau_4 = \frac{\lambda_4}{\lambda_2}$; sample version from unbiased probability-weighted moments.
The trimmed L-moment ratio $\tau_3^{(1)}$ with trimming (1,1), which exists without moments.
The trimmed L-moment ratio $\tau_4^{(1)}$ with trimming (1,1).

Bowley's quartile skewness $\frac{Q_3 + Q_1 - 2Q_2}{Q_3 - Q_1}$, the member at $u = \frac{1}{4}$ of the quantile skewness family of Groeneveld & Meeden (1984); sample quartiles by linear interpolation (R type 7).
The medcouple, a robust skewness measure in $[-1, 1]$ built from the median of a kernel over pairs of values on either side of the median.

Skewness centred at the mean, $2F(\mu_1) - 1$ ($F$ the distribution function), bounded in $[-1, 1]$ and positive for right-skewed distributions, the same sign convention as moment skewness; the bounded form used by Eberl & Klar (2020) of Tajuddin's (1996) log-odds $\log\frac{F(\mu_1)}{1 - F(\mu_1)}$. Sample version $2\hat F(m_1) - 1$, the share of values at or below the sample mean, rescaled.
Moors octile kurtosis $\frac{(E_7 - E_5) + (E_3 - E_1)}{E_6 - E_2}$, $E_k$ the $k$-th octile; sample octiles by R type 7.
The ratio of the mean absolute deviation to the standard deviation, $\frac{\mathrm{E}|y-\mu_1|}{\sigma}$, the order-one analogue of Hypotailedness.

The coefficients built on the half central moment that the study compares with other measures: [[D3:Asymmetry coefficient]], [[D4:Hypotailedness]], [[D5:Extremity coefficient]] and [[D8:Complex Extremity]].

The measures the half-moment coefficients are compared with: for skewness, [[D9:moment skewness]], [[D11:L-skewness]], [[D13:TL-skewness]], [[D15:quartile skewness]], [[D16:medcouple]] and [[D17:mean-based skewness]]; for tail weight, [[D10:excess kurtosis]], [[D12:L-kurtosis]], [[D14:TL-kurtosis]], [[D18:octile kurtosis]] and [[D19:Geary ratio]].

Samples of size $n$ drawn from a base distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$; in each, the first value is replaced by $\mu + k\sigma$. Every measure is computed on the clean sample and on the contaminated one.

For one measure, base distribution, $n$ and $k$: the mean over replications of the measure on the contaminated samples minus its mean on the clean samples, divided by the standard deviation of the measure over the clean samples.
Measurements on 48 rock samples from a petroleum reservoir (BP research), the rock data set of R's datasets package: area, perimeter, shape and permeability.

Daily closing prices of four European stock indices (DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE), 1991-1998, business days, 1860 observations each: the EuStockMarkets data set of R's datasets package; analysed as daily log returns (1859 each).
Every measure computed on the first $t$ returns of a series, for every $t$ from 30 to the full length.

claims.statement: The variable $y$ has a finite mean $\mu_1$.
The variable $y$ has a finite, positive variance $\sigma^2$.

For a variable with a finite positive variance $\sigma^2$, let $V = \frac{(y - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma^2}$, the squared standardised deviation, whose mean is 1, and $g(v) = \frac{3 + v}{4} - v^{0.25}$. Then one minus the [[D4:Hypotailedness]] equals $\mathrm{E}[g(V)]$, the [[D5:Extremity coefficient]] equals $2(1 - \mathrm{E}[g(V)])^p - 1$ and so decreases as $\mathrm{E}[g(V)]$ grows, and, with a finite fourth moment, the [[D10:excess kurtosis]] plus 2 equals $\mathrm{E}[(V - 1)^2]$. The function $g$ is strictly convex and zero only at $v = 1$, is $\frac{3}{32}(v - 1)^2 + O(|v - 1|^3)$ near 1, is $\frac{3}{4}$ at $v = 0$, and is $\frac{v}{4} + O(v^{0.25})$ for large $v$. So Hypotailedness, Extremity and kurtosis all measure how far $V$ spreads from 1; with $g$ scaled by $\frac{32}{3}$, so that it agrees with the kurtosis loss $(v - 1)^2$ to second order at $v = 1$, Hypotailedness gives a value at the mean 8 times the weight kurtosis gives it, and a value far out a weight linear rather than quadratic in $V$.

checks.notes: Checked every step of proofs/properties.md section H20 against the recorded wording of H20, by hand and numerically. (1) E[V] = E[D^2]/sigma^2 = 1; |D|^0.5 = (D^2)^(1/4), so H = E[V^(1/4)] (TM4 definition). Integrability: E V = 1 and 0 <= V^(1/4) <= 1 + V, so each term of g(V) is integrable and linearity gives E[g(V)] = (3+1)/4 - H = 1 - H. Holds. (2) Extremity = 2H^p - 1 = 2(1 - E[g(V)])^p - 1 by TM5; p = log 0.5/log(2*3^-0.75) = 5.2988 > 0 and 1 - E[g(V)] = H lies in (0,1] (H7, which I re-derived: Jensen with r = 1/4), so u -> 2u^p - 1 is strictly increasing there and Extremity is strictly decreasing in E[g(V)] over its whole range [0,1). Holds. (3) With E[D^4] finite, E[V^2] = E[D^4]/sigma^4 = kappa, so E[(V-1)^2] = kappa - 2 + 1 = kappa - 1 = excess kurtosis (TM10) + 2. Holds. (4) g'(v) = (1 - v^(-3/4))/4, g''(v) = (3/16) v^(-7/4) > 0 on (0,inf), confirmed by differentiation. The proof passes from this to strict convexity on the closed [0,inf) by continuity at 0 in one clause; that step is correct (g' strictly increasing on (0,inf) plus the mean value theorem on [0,c] and [c,b] gives strict chord inequality for chords starting at 0, although g'(0+) = -inf), but the text does not spell it out. (5) g(1) = 0, g'(1) = 0, strict convexity gives g(v) > 0 for every v != 1 in [0,inf), including v = 0. Holds. (6) Taylor at 1: g''(1)/2 = 3/32; g'''(v) = -(21/64) v^(-11/4) is bounded near 1, so the remainder is O(|v-1|^3); the cubic coefficient is -7/128. Holds. (7) g(0) = 3/4 = 24/32 = 8 * (3/32)(0-1)^2. Holds. (8) g(v) - v/4 = 3/4 - v^(1/4) = O(v^(1/4)) as v -> inf. Holds. Numeric checks (scratch script outside the repository): for normal, uniform, exponential, t(5) and beta(0.5,2), 1 - H and E[g(V)] agree to 1e-12 and excess kurtosis + 2 equals E[(V-1)^2]; uniform gives Extremity 0; g on a grid over [0,1e4] has its only zero at 1; (g(1+h) - (3/32)h^2)/h^3 tends to -0.0547 = -7/128; (g(v) - v/4)/v^(1/4) tends to -1; 1e6 random chords, 30 percent starting at v = 0, show no convexity violation. Nothing wrong found; no step missing that affects the result. Closing interpretive sentence: a fair reading, not an overstatement, under two qualifications that the statement leaves implicit. First, 'measure how far V spreads from 1' is supported in this exact sense: 1 - Hypotailedness and excess kurtosis + 2 are each the mean of a non-negative loss of V that is zero only at V = 1, so each is 0 exactly when V = 1 almost surely, and Extremity is a strictly decreasing function of the first; Hypotailedness and Extremity themselves fall as the spread grows. It does not say, and the proof does not show, that the two losses order distributions the same way (they do not: exponential and t(5) have the same kurtosis 9 but E[g(V)] 0.2121 and 0.2245). Second, '8 times more' and 'linearly rather than quadratically' are comparisons with the kurtosis loss (v-1)^2 scaled by 3/32 so that the two losses agree to second order at v = 1; the factor 8 depends on that choice of scaling, which the statement indicates only through the expression 8 times (3/32)(0-1)^2. With that scaling the comparison is exact: g(0) = 3/4 against 3/32, and g(v) ~ v/4 against (3/32)v^2. (2) For p > 0, u -> 2u^p - 1 is continuous and strictly increasing on [0,1], sending 0 to -1 and 1 to 1; correct. (3) h_U^p = exp(log 0.5) = 0.5, so h_U maps to 0; verified to 30 digits. (4) By H23 (which I checked separately and confirmed) H is in (0,1]; strict monotonicity gives E > -1 and E <= 1, and E < 0 iff H < h_U; correct. (5) H10 re-derived: for the uniform law on (b,c), a = (c-b)/2, nu = (2/3)a^0.5, sigma^2 = a^2/3, H = (2/3)*3^0.25 = 2*3^-0.75 = h_U, so E = 0; confirmed by quadrature for three intervals (differences below 1e-24). Nothing wrong. One remark on wording, not an error: 'the uniform distribution' means the continuous uniform law on an interval, as in H10; a discrete uniform law has a different H.

evidence.description: Lab runs RN12 under plan PL3. Design: Single-outlier contamination: base distributions normal(0,1), Student t(5) and exponential(1); sample sizes n = 100 and 1000; 10000 replications for each base distribution and n, the same clean samples reused for every k; in each sample the first value replaced by mu + k sigma, k = 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100; seeds fixed (seed 20261120 for the first base distribution and n, incremented for each next one). Every measure of the half-moment coefficients and of the comparison measures is computed on each clean and each contaminated sample. Analysis: For each measure, base distribution, n and k: the standardised shift (mean over replications of the measure on contaminated samples minus its mean on clean samples, divided by its standard deviation on clean samples) with its Monte Carlo standard error; and for each measure, base distribution and n, the growth exponent: the slope of log |standardised shift| on log k over k = 10, 20, 50, 100, to set beside the influence functions of H17 (Q1).

evidence.description: Lab runs RN13 under plan PL6. Design: Samples from the normal(0,1), Student t(5) and exponential(1) distributions, n = 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 and 2000; 10000 replications for each distribution and n (seed 20261122, incremented for each next one). On each sample: the sample Asymmetry, Hypotailedness, Extremity and both parts of the Complex Extremity; 95% intervals for each by (a) the normal approximation with a jackknife standard error and (b) the percentile bootstrap with 999 resamples, the bootstrap on the first 2000 replications only. Analysis: For each coefficient, distribution and n: bias (mean minus true value), standard deviation, root mean squared error and sqrt(n) times the standard deviation, each with its Monte Carlo standard error; coverage of the two 95% intervals with its Monte Carlo standard error.

How far one moved value shifts each measure. The first value of a sample of n = 1000 is replaced by the mean plus k standard deviations; each line is a measure's standardised shift (absolute value) against k, for normal, Student t (5 degrees of freedom) and exponential samples, on logarithmic axes. The slope of a line at large k is the measure's growth exponent: excess kurtosis and moment skewness climb fastest, Hypotailedness next, Asymmetry and Extremity at about the rate of L-skewness and L-kurtosis, and the medcouple stays flat.

Excess kurtosis (top) and the Extremity coefficient (bottom) of the DAX daily log returns, 1991-1998, each computed on the first t returns for every t from 30 to 1859. Excess kurtosis peaks at 50.2 at 266 returns and ends at 6.3; Extremity stays between -0.927 and -0.175, reaching both extremes within the first 37 returns, and changes slowly afterwards.

Bias (top) and coverage of the 95% interval with a jackknife standard error (bottom) of the sample Asymmetry, Hypotailedness and Extremity against the sample size n, for normal, Student t (5 degrees of freedom) and exponential samples, 10000 replications each; grey lines mark zero bias and 95% coverage. Asymmetry is nearly unbiased and covers close to 95%; Extremity and Hypotailedness are biased upwards in small samples and their intervals under-cover for the heavier-tailed and skewed distributions.
